comments.author: irishloop
comments.text:
I think a lot of people here seem to underestimate how much of a CEO's job is perception.
"Oh who cares who he slept with, he's been great for Nvidia. Nothing has been proven."
He's one of the most visible CEO's in the most visible industry in the world, and the entire AI economy is dependent upon them. The perception of him as stable is incredibly important.
Merely the suggestion that he is having affairs with people with close ties to China's government, given export controls, is a huge PR problem. Adding in an additional affair with someone under him. And the likelihood that there may be even more out there.
I doubt the Board wants to get rid of Jensen Huang. He's done incredibly well for them. But right now, there's a huge PR shitstorm swirling around the company.
Maybe in six months it all dies down and he comes back, who knows. But right now, you really can't just ignore the problem and hope the media doesn't care about the whole "well she was only sort of a spy" situation.

comments.author: amluto
comments.text:
Wow, in my mind this is beyond “code smell” and into code reek!
According to the article, Postgres has an internal Datum that might be a pointer or not a pointer. Okay, this is already a bit risky.
Datum comes along with a small-integer type id.  That id is stored separately, presumably for efficiency? Maybe you have lots of Datums and one id and you do this for efficiency. Okay, as long as there is a clear story for why the id stays correctly bound to the datum. The “internal” thing where a bogus AST will cause type confusion makes me think the story here isn’t great.
But then I learn that the type id is something that the code
looks up in a system table in the database
.  I’m speechless.  This is the kind of thing that
can’t
be represented in any safe language because
the indication of whether a value is a pointer isn’t even in application memory.
Eww.  Maybe the AIs can exhaustively enumerate every code path that might get it wrong and rule them all out in a particular release. Maybe there’s even a Lean program that can verify it. But this is still the kind of design that is wrong by construction and is only okay if every single detail avoids the giant foot-cannon.

For the last five months or so, opus and fable have both been able to do this task as a soneshot prompt. An inference engine is almost pure compute and to a first approximation the only operation your hardware needs to support to do llm inference is multiplication [the rest of an inference engine is "some trig"].
So to get any model working on $OLD_HARDWARE, the hardest part of the task is now sourcing the hardware itself and giving the agent ssh access -- a modern agent will be able to source a compiler, write the implementation, optimize it, test in qemu (or any other simulator) and push it onto the device.
Example prompt: "write an inference engine for qwen3 0.6b in pure assembly that runs on this device. Write a script to attach the weights to the resulting binary. Prefix is supplied as a stream of u32 token IDs on stdin. The engine streams u32 token IDs on stdout."
